title: Psychiatrist says he didn't believe Stochmal was dangerous
article: Less than an hour after the stabbing on the night of Sept. 1, 2001, a frenzied and struggling Stochmal, who required six police officers to subdue him and take him into custody after being handcuffed, pepper sprayed and having his feet hobbled and tied to his wrist-cuffs by a pair of handcuffs, was dead.
He suffered cardiac arrest while being placed in the back of a police cruiser and attempts to revive him at the scene and en route to hospital were unsuccessful.

Jurors at the inquest heard that Stochmal visited the Regina Mental Health Clinic at his wife's insistence on Aug. 31, 2001 and saw Dr. Sanjeev Sharma. Sharma diagnosed the 35-year-old man, who suffers from a bipolar disorder (mood swings disorder) as manic and experiencing anxiety.

"Bipolar disorder is not associated with violent behaviour and it is very uncommon for them to display aggressive behaviour," Sharma said, explaining people in a manic state are usually euphoric and have exaggerated, grandiose ideas.
In Stochmal's case, he talked about God, how he was going to write a book, and how he was going to change the world. "He had a belief that he had the power to make the world a better place."
However, he said, "this disease is very unpredictable and once you lose touch with reality a person's behaviour can become unpredictable (psychotic)."
The psychiatrist also explained that under the Mental Health Services Act, Stochmal didn't meet the criteria needed for an involuntary certification and committal to hospital.
"His speech was rapid and rambling, but he said he wasn't hearing voices or seeing anything at the time I spoke to him," Sharma said.
Nor did he articulate or display any visible signs of violent tendencies or malaise toward his wife and children, Sharma told the inquest.

His illness hadn't progressed to the point where in-patient care was his only option, he was able to make an informed decision about his care and treatment as an out-patient, and Sharma said Stochmal wasn't considered a threat to himself or others.

Stochmal refused to be voluntarily hospitalized, but agreed to take anti-psychotic medication, Sharma said, explaining he provided his patient with samples of the anti-depression, mood-stabilization drug in the hopes Stochmal would comply with the out-patient treatment and take his medication.
"Medication is the best treatment for this disorder. The only benefits of hospitalization is to ensure that the patients are taking their medication," he said.
Stochmal's father had agreed to monitor his son over the weekend to ensure he was taking his medication, Sharma said, explaining he had arranged a follow-up appointment Sept. 5.
Had he been made aware of any safety concerns, Sharma said, that would have been a determining factor in his decision whether to hospitalize Stochmal.
